title: no blank mind required
hook: meditation isn't clearing your mind; the word spirit means breath
tomorrow: the tattoo that's really about today

segments.voice: Yesterday: meant to be, and the question that always has an answer: not why, but what now. Today, a word hiding inside spiritual.

The line that makes people quit meditating is clear your mind. They sit down, the mind does the opposite, and they decide they're bad at it. If that's you, here's the good news. Nobody's mind goes blank on command, and the old teachers didn't ask it to. They asked for something much smaller. And you don't have to believe anything to start.

Spiritual comes from the Latin spiritus, which means breath. Inspire once meant to breathe into; expire, to breathe out for the last time. Greek, Hebrew and Sanskrit each have a word that means breath and spirit at once. So the spiritual in spiritual but not religious starts, at its root, with breathing. Now the technique, the way breath meditation is actually taught. Feel one breath: cool air at the nose, the belly rising. Within a few breaths the mind wanders off: an email, a song, an argument from Tuesday. Then, at some point, you notice. That moment of noticing isn't the failure. It's the practice. In 1890 the psychologist William James wrote that "bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." Over and over. Wander, notice, come back: that's one rep, like lifting a weight. A mind that wanders twenty times in a minute just did twenty reps. And breath has one more trick. You can't slow your heart by deciding to. You can slow your breath, and a long breath out tends to settle the body.
screen: `SPIRITUS — BREATH.` · `FEEL ONE BREATH.` · `WANDER, NOTICE, COME BACK.` · `EVERY RETURN IS A REP.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in slowly and feel where the air goes. Let it out a little longer than it came in. If a thought shows up halfway, that's fine. Notice it, and finish the breath. That's one rep.
Breathe. The root under the word spirit, and the place you come back to. Second word on your strand.
Your line: wander, notice, come back. The wandering is part of it, not proof you're bad at it. Day two, done.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TATTOO THAT'S REALLY ABOUT TODAY.`

howItsDone: Breath meditation is taught on many paths, Buddhist, Hindu and secular alike: rest attention on the breath, notice when it wanders, and gently bring it back, as many times as it takes.

fork.setup: you sit for one minute and your mind wanders off ten times. by William James's account, what did you just do?
options: bring attention back ten times: the root of the skill.
fork.reveal: "bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again" is the skill itself. ten wanders, ten returns.

original.note: Latin, from spirare, to breathe. English spirit, inspire and expire all come from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: air in, air out. and meditation means a blank mind.
what it means: the root of spirit, and the place a wandering mind comes back to.

what a scholar hears: Latin spiritus, from spirare; Greek pneuma, Hebrew ruach and Sanskrit prana each join breath and spirit. James 1890, chapter XI: bringing back a wandering attention is 'the very root of judgment, character, and will.'

story.title: the man who stopped forcing it
story.text: A man has starved himself so long that when he touches his belly he can feel his backbone. For years he has tried every hard way to force his mind still, and none has worked. Then he remembers being a boy, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, when a deep calm came over him without any effort at all. Maybe, he thinks, that's the way. He eats a real meal, and his five companions walk off in disgust. He's the man people would come to call the Buddha.
story.source: early Buddhist texts: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta)

wrong.truth: breath meditation asks you to feel the breath, notice when you've wandered, and come back. the coming back is the practice.

think.setup: your sister, who's devout, is worried your meditation is opening a door to something bad. you feel scared and a little hurt. what's a kind first move?
options: tell her plainly what you do: one breath, noticed, and ask what worries her.
hide it from her from now on.
think.reveal: worry like hers usually comes from love. saying plainly what the practice is, a breath and a return, tends to help more than a debate. you can belong to each other and still see things differently.
